messages.job: Get an honest 1-5 rating and route unhappy customers away from the public review ask.
messages.does: Asks for a 1-5 rating with a reply and invites what would have made it a 5, gating the rest of the sequence.
messages.quote: 1 to 5, how did we do?

messages.job: Ask a customer who already rated the experience highly to leave a public Google review, tying it to helping the next homeowner.
messages.does: Uses Feel-Felt-Found empathy (you were once searching for who to trust) and asks for a review, gated to the 'Happy Ask' branch, with no incentive offered.
messages.quote: I read every one. Your perspective matters to me.

messages.job: Nudge the same happy customer toward the review link shortly after the email, standing on its own.
messages.does: Repeats the 'you were once figuring this out' framing with the review link, five minutes after the email.
messages.quote: A few weeks ago you were figuring this out.

messages.job: Give a final, low-pressure reminder to leave a review to a happy customer who hasn't yet.
messages.does: Reminds them they're now the homeowner others look to and repeats the review link, with no pressure language.
messages.quote: your review would go a long way:

summary.strategy: Ask a happy customer to send a referral, framed as a casual, low-pressure nudge instead of a formal ask.
summary.angle: You're already the person your neighbors ask about windows, just point them our way.
summary.why: Both paths keep the ask low-pressure, standalone, and compliant, with no incentive offered and no fake urgency.

messages.job: Ask a happy customer for a referral, framed as a casual thought rather than a formal solicitation.
messages.does: Suggests they probably already have a friend in mind and asks them to send that person Reece's way.
messages.quote: If that person comes to mind, send them our way.

messages.job: Ask the same referral question with a neighborhood-specific angle for customers further past their install (30+ days).
messages.does: Notes neighbors start asking once one home upgrades and invites them to connect a neighbor who's asked or seems close.
messages.quote: Once one home on the street upgrades, people start noticing and asking.

summary.strategy: As written, thank the customer for leaving a review, then ask them for a referral three times.
summary.angle: You already told us we did a good job, now help someone else find us.
summary.momentum_break: C.6-S02 (Day +2) — the workflow drops the review-amplifier job entirely and becomes a second referral-ask sequence, duplicating C.5 Referral Overlay.
summary.why: Only S01 does what a review amplifier should do (thank the customer, catch any problem). S02 and S03 are referral asks wearing Review Amplifier's name, sending the same content C.5 already owns, so a customer touched by both workflows could get near-identical referral asks twice in the same window.

messages.job: Thank the customer for leaving a review and give a safety-net way to flag anything that could have gone better.
messages.does: Thanks them, explains the review helps other local families, and invites a reply if anything could have gone better.
messages.quote: Thank you for taking a minute on that review.

messages.job: Amplify the review just left (thank them further, invite them to share it wider, or reinforce the value of their voice), the job a 'Review Amplifier' step should do.
messages.does: Pivots straight into a referral ask ('send us their name and number') instead of amplifying the review.
messages.quote: has been putting their windows off, send us their name and number.
messages.issue: C.6 is named and formulated (F12-review) as a review amplifier, but S02 asks for a referral instead of amplifying the review. This is the exact job C.5 Referral Overlay already owns, so a customer tagged into both could get a near-identical referral ask from two different workflows.
messages.recommendation: Rewrite S02 to amplify the review itself (thank them again, ask permission to feature it, or invite a second-platform review) and let C.5 own every referral ask.

messages.job: Close out the review-amplifier sequence with a final thank-you, not a third solicitation.
messages.does: Makes a third referral ask before landing on a thank-you close.
messages.quote: thank you again for trusting us with your home.
messages.issue: A third consecutive message doing C.5's referral-ask job instead of C.6's own review-amplifier job; by the third ask in a row it also risks reading as pressure on a customer who already gave what was originally asked (a review).
messages.recommendation: Replace the referral ask with a genuine review-amplifier close (thank them, offer to feature their review/photos) and retire the referral cadence into C.5 alone.

summary.strategy: When a customer mentions someone they'd refer, capture that lead's contact info quickly and with zero pressure, then let it go.
summary.angle: You already offered, we're just making it easy to follow through.
summary.why: formulas.md's deployment matrix lists C.7 as 'no copy (capture)', but three real SMS nudges exist and they do exactly the low-pressure capture job the workflow name promises: no pitch, no education, an easy off-ramp on the last message ('if not, no problem'). Worth flagging to whoever maintains formulas.md that the matrix entry doesn't match what's actually live; the copy itself is compliant.

messages.job: Capture the name/number of a referral the customer already volunteered, quickly and with no pressure.
messages.does: Confirms it heard the customer mention someone, asks for at least a first name, and offers the option to just hand over the business number instead.
messages.quote: Even just a first name is fine.

messages.job: Give a low-pressure nudge to capture the referral's info if it wasn't sent yet.
messages.does: Says no rush and asks again for a name, framing it as easy on both sides.
messages.quote: No rush, but if you want to send over a name for the neighbor or friend you mentioned

messages.job: Make one final, pressure-free attempt to capture the referral before letting it go.
messages.does: Says this is the last nudge and offers a fallback of just passing along Reece's number whenever it comes up.
messages.quote: Last nudge on this one.

summary.strategy: Welcome someone who just downloaded the Risk Report, confirm they're in good hands, and open a curiosity loop for Randy's daily field notes — without selling anything yet.
summary.angle: You already pulled your Risk Report; here's what it can't show you, and Randy will walk you through it one story at a time.
summary.momentum_break: SMS #1 (fallback, non-AI version) — the workflow's own AI prompt for this exact touch explicitly forbids a booking link ('NO CTA... No booking link'), but the stored fallback text used when the AI doesn't fire includes one, plus a direct reference to the email.
summary.why: The Randy email and the intended rep SMS are a clean stage-1 welcome with no pitch. But the actual fallback SMS text on file breaks the workflow's own no-CTA rule and references the email directly, so a real lead can get a premature booking push on day 0 depending on which branch fires.

messages.job: Welcome the reader after they downloaded the Risk Report, validate the download as smart, and open one curiosity loop about the next few notes — no pitch.
messages.does: Confirms the report, honestly says it shows a pattern but not their specific gap, and promises daily field stories from Randy over 5 days, with a soft reply invite and no CTA.
messages.quote: the Risk Report surfaces a gap PATTERN — the same pattern Florida homes share when documented protection is incomplete.

messages.job: Introduce the rep as the point of contact and invite practical questions — a second, human channel alongside Randy's notes.
messages.does: Introduces the rep by name, but the prompt tells the model to restate that the reader 'should have just received their Risk Report and Randy's intro note' — pointing the text back at the email that just went out.
messages.quote: You should have your Risk Report and Randy's intro note. He'll send a short note each day for about a week.
messages.issue: The prompt has the SMS restate what was in the email ('should have your Risk Report and Randy's intro note'), which is the sms_standalone failure the rubric flags even without saying 'I just sent you an email.'
messages.recommendation: Drop the reference to the email's contents; let the SMS stand on its own, e.g. introduce the rep and invite a reply about anything in the report, without naming what Randy already sent.

messages.job: Same as the AI-written rep intro: introduce the rep, no pitch, no booking link (this is the fallback text used when the AI version doesn't generate).
messages.does: Introduces the rep, but also says 'just sent your Risk Report to your email' (referencing the email directly) and adds a booking link to 'have an expert evaluate your home's protection level' on the very first contact.
messages.quote: If you already want an expert to evaluate your home's protection level, grab a time here
messages.issue: This fallback SMS undoes the workflow's own 'NO CTA' rule for the welcome touch (see the Email #1 prompt) by adding a booking link on day 0, and it directly references the email ('just sent your Risk Report to your email'), which also fails sms_standalone.
messages.recommendation: Match the fallback text to the AI prompt's own rule: introduce the rep, invite a reply about the report, and drop the booking link until later in the sequence.

summary.strategy: For leads who started the online calculator and stalled, offer to do the measuring for them in person instead of asking them to finish it.
summary.angle: You don't have to finish the calculator — we'll come measure your actual home and give you the real number.
summary.why: Per Mark's ruling, calculator leads can book the in-home visit directly rather than going through the Protection Profile Review first, and this is exactly that: a calculator flow booking its own in-home step. All three touches stay on-topic (convenience, not brand positioning), carry no compliance flags, and the copy matches the workflow's stated job.

messages.job: Recover a lead who stalled mid-calculator by offering a lower-effort path to the same answer, with no sales pressure.
messages.does: Names the exact stall point (window sizes), then offers to send a rep out to measure instead, with a link.
messages.quote: We can come measure everything for you, free, and give you the accurate number based on your actual home. Want to go that route instead?

messages.job: Second, lower-pressure nudge repeating the same no-homework offer for someone who didn't respond to the first text.
messages.does: Restates the swap (visit instead of calculator) in fewer words, with the same link.
messages.quote: The home visit replaces the calculator - we measure everything, give you the accurate number, and you decide.

messages.job: Final, low-pressure nudge before the thread goes quiet — give one more concrete reason (speed and accuracy) to take the easier path.
messages.does: Frames the home visit as faster and more accurate than the calculator, then closes the thread with the link.
messages.quote: the home visit is usually faster than trying to estimate everything manually — and the number is more accurate because we can see things the calculator can't

summary.strategy: Follow up on a chatbot conversation to keep the lead warm, opening curiosity loops about code compliance and window ratings.
summary.angle: There's one detail about your home's protection that didn't come up in the chat — here's why it matters.
summary.momentum_break: Email #2 (Belief Shift — Hidden Vulnerability) — introduces an invented $45,000 Tampa claim-denial figure that isn't an allowed stat and collides with the locked Tampa $28,000 parable, and repeats the 'South Florida' default market from Email #1.
summary.why: The stage-fit is mostly right (curiosity, no pitch) but two emails default to 'South Florida' instead of {{contact.city}}, one predicts a specific insurance-claim outcome, and one invents an unauthorized $45,000 stat that conflicts with the locked Tampa parable. The final no-email SMS also turns into a primary booking push.

messages.job: Acknowledge the chat and open a curiosity loop about something tailored to them, without pitching anything.
messages.does: References the earlier chat and offers to send something useful if they reply with their email.
messages.quote: I put together something useful for you based on what you shared, mind if I send it to your email?

messages.job: Standalone relevance hook for someone who didn't answer the first text — give a reason the topic matters, no ask beyond a soft nudge.
messages.does: Raises Florida's updated code requirement as a reason homeowners get caught out, ends with a soft suggestion to check.
messages.quote: Florida updated their building code requirements again recently. A lot of homeowners who thought they were compliant found out the hard way during inspections.

messages.job: Close out the SMS-only thread with one last, low-pressure option, keeping the door open rather than pushing.
messages.does: Offers a 'free... assessment' and a booking link as the entire content of the final message to a cold, no-email chat lead.
messages.quote: If you ever want a quick professional assessment of your windows, free, no pressure, just reply "check" or grab a time here:
messages.issue: This makes the booking link the whole message to a stage-1 reader who's had two low-commitment texts and no story or trust-building — it's a primary CTA, not the P.S./footer-level escape hatch the framework calls for at this trust level. 'Free... assessment' also echoes the banned 'free estimate/inspection' pattern.
messages.recommendation: Keep the reply option ('reply check') but drop the direct booking link at this trust level, or move it to a P.S. instead of being the whole ask.

messages.job: Follow up on the chat with something that didn't come up, opening a curiosity loop about the one detail that matters most — no positioning yet.
messages.does: Opens with 'South Florida' as the default market instead of the lead's own city, and predicts that the detail determines 'whether your insurance claim gets paid.'
messages.quote: whether your insurance claim gets paid, whether your home passes inspection, and whether your family is actually safe when it matters.
messages.issue: Two compliance breaks: the subject/opening line defaults to 'South Florida' instead of {{contact.city}} (the email does use {{contact.city}} once later, but the lead line sets the wrong default), and the body predicts a specific insurance outcome ('whether your insurance claim gets paid'), which is a hard line regardless of stage.
messages.recommendation: Replace 'South Florida homeowners' with {{contact.city}} homeowners, and rewrite the claim-paid line to something the company can actually promise — e.g. 'whether your documentation holds up' — not a prediction of the insurer's decision.

messages.job: Standalone emotional hook that opens a curiosity loop about the window rating, independent of the email that went out the same window.
messages.does: Asks a direct question about window rating and frames it as the #1 thing insurers check, without referencing the email.
messages.quote: do you know what rating your windows have? It's the #1 thing insurers check after a storm, and most homeowners have no idea.

messages.job: Reveal the secret (certification for YOUR zone, not just 'having impact windows') through a story, no brand positioning.
messages.does: Tells a Tampa homeowner's claim-denial story with a $45,000 figure, and again defaults to 'South Florida' instead of the lead's own city.
messages.quote: a homeowner in Tampa filed a $45,000 wind damage claim. Impact windows installed. Shutters on every opening. They did everything right
messages.issue: The $45,000 figure isn't one of the five allowed stats, and it puts a specific claim-denial dollar amount on a Tampa story — the locked Tampa parable is $28,000, so this invents a conflicting number for the same city. 'South Florida' also appears again as the default market.
messages.recommendation: Use the actual $3,800 (no-city) or Tampa $28,000 parable as written, or a true unnamed story with no invented dollar figure; replace 'South Florida' with {{contact.city}}.

messages.job: Standalone urgency seed reinforcing the code-change relevance beat, no reference to the paired email.
messages.does: Repeats the code-update fact as a quick, standalone heads-up.
messages.quote: Florida updated their building code requirements again. Homes that were compliant last year might not be anymore.

summary.strategy: Follow up on a door-knock with something relevant to the reader's own street, building curiosity about a code-compliance gap without pitching.
summary.angle: We noticed something about the homes on your street while we were out there.
summary.momentum_break: Email #2 (Neighborhood Risk Awareness, day 1) — signs as 'Mark from Reece' before any appointment, and tells a $45,000 claim-denial story that isn't an allowed stat and duplicates the same figure used for a different city elsewhere in the funnel.
summary.why: Most of the sequence is a clean relevance-building bridge for a cold canvassing lead. But one SMS predicts a specific claim-paid/denied outcome, one email is sent from Mark pre-appointment (a voice reserved for after the appointment) and tells an invented $45,000 claim story, and the final SMS turns the entire message into a booking push under a mislabeled 'free... phone review.'

messages.job: Acknowledge the door visit and make the topic relevant to the reader's own street, offering a low-commitment lead magnet — no pitch.
messages.does: References the visit, teases a street-specific finding, and offers the free guide in exchange for an email.
messages.quote: After walking your street, we noticed something about the homes in {{contact.city}} that most homeowners don't know about. We put together a free Hurricane Preparedness Guide that covers it.

messages.job: Follow-up relevance hook naming a concrete reason (a pre-2007 build) the topic applies, still no pitch.
messages.does: Names the 2007 code-cutoff detail and offers the guide again.
messages.quote: if your home was built or renovated before 2007, there's a good chance it doesn't meet the current Florida hurricane protection code.

messages.job: Final soft close for a cold canvassing lead, keeping the option open without pressure.
messages.does: Makes the entire final message a booking push described as 'a free 10-minute phone review' (not the locked 'Protection Profile Review' name) plus an unverified '2x the cost' figure.
messages.quote: we do a free 10-minute phone review. No sales pitch. Just answers. Reply "check" or grab a time:
messages.issue: The whole message is a direct CTA to a cold, day-1, stage-1 reader instead of a footnote escape hatch, and it names the review generically ('free... phone review') rather than the locked 'Protection Profile Review.' '2x the cost' is also an unverified figure outside the five allowed stats.
messages.recommendation: Rename the call as the 'Protection Profile Review' and drop '2x the cost'; keep the ask as a soft, optional reply rather than the whole message.

messages.job: Same as SMS #1 for a contact missing city data — acknowledge the visit, tease a finding, offer the guide.
messages.does: Uses a generic 'your area' in place of the missing city and offers the guide.
messages.quote: {{text_formatter.1.result}} stopped by your place earlier - appreciate you taking a minute. After walking your street, we noticed something about the homes in your area that most homeowners don't know about.

messages.job: Same as SMS #1 for a contact whose name wasn't captured (uses a generic 'guys' reference in place of the rep name).
messages.does: Acknowledges the visit informally and offers the guide.

messages.job: Same as SMS #1 for a contact with neither name nor city captured.
messages.does: Acknowledges the visit generically and offers the guide.
messages.quote: {{text_formatter.1.result}} stopped by your place earlier - appreciate you taking a minute. After walking your street, we noticed something about the homes in your area that most homeowners don't know about.

messages.job: Follow up on the door visit with the part that didn't come up, opening a curiosity loop about the code-compliance detail — no pitch.
messages.does: Makes the topic relevant to the reader's own street and city, promises a follow-up on how to check it, no CTA.
messages.quote: a lot of the homes in {{contact.city}} were built or renovated before the current Florida building code took effect.

messages.job: Standalone emotional hook about window rating, independent of the paired email.
messages.does: Asks whether the reader knows their window rating, but states as fact that it 'determines whether your insurance claim gets paid.'
messages.quote: It's the number one thing that determines whether your insurance claim gets paid after a storm.
messages.issue: This predicts a specific insurance-claim outcome (whether a claim gets paid), which is a hard compliance line regardless of how well the stage-fit otherwise works.
messages.recommendation: Rephrase to what's actually true and checkable, e.g. 'it's one of the first things an insurer looks at after a storm' rather than a payout guarantee/denial claim.

messages.job: Deepen the relevance/curiosity loop about the certification-vs-record gap with a concrete story, still no brand pitch.
messages.does: Tells a Broward family's story about a denied $45,000 claim, sent from 'Mark from Reece' rather than Randy.
messages.quote: They filed a $45,000 claim and it was denied.
messages.issue: This email is sent 'from: Mark from Reece' before any appointment has happened — Mark's first-person voice is only approved after the appointment; Randy is the pre-appointment voice. The $45,000 figure also isn't one of the five allowed stats, and it's the same invented number used for a different city (Tampa) in E.3's Email #2, which suggests a recycled, unverified claim-denial story.
messages.recommendation: Send this from Randy (or the generic rep voice) instead of Mark pre-appointment, and replace the invented $45,000 figure with a true, verifiable stat or a properly-attributed parable.

messages.job: Standalone urgency seed reinforcing the code-change relevance beat ahead of storm season, independent of the email.
messages.does: Repeats the code-update fact and points at storm season as a real, upcoming reason to check.
messages.quote: Florida raised the hurricane protection requirements again. Homes that were fully compliant a few years ago might not be anymore.

summary.strategy: Catch-all welcome for leads with no known source: build curiosity about a certification-vs-record mismatch over 5 days, then offer the 15-minute Protection Profile Review.
summary.angle: There's one number on your windows most homeowners have never actually been shown — here's what it is and where the mismatch usually shows up.
summary.why: Structural finding, not a copy problem: 3,362 leads entered in 30 days and every step shows 0 sends — the messages aren't going out. The copy itself is the strongest in this batch (correct Review naming throughout, one true unnamed story with no invented figures), but two of the seven messages still predict a specific insurance-coverage outcome and should be fixed before the trigger is re-enabled.

messages.job: Be relevant enough to keep the number from being blocked and open a curiosity loop before the email lands.
messages.does: Opens the curiosity loop ('one number'), then points at the email that's coming.
messages.quote: One number that shows what your home was engineered to handle. Short version in a bit.
messages.issue: 'Short version in a bit' points the text at the coming email rather than standing fully on its own (mechanical sms_standalone rule; ruled a fail, not a fault of the stage-fit — Mark, 2026-09-25).
messages.recommendation: Drop the forward reference to the email; end on the curiosity loop alone.

messages.job: Make the impact rating feel relevant/critical (F1) without positioning Reece; open the loop Randy will keep filling.
messages.does: Explains the impact rating in Randy's voice, lists four things it can quietly affect, and closes with a P.S. escape-hatch link to the Protection Profile Review — the correct locked name, placed as a footer, not the primary ask.
messages.quote: what your insurance company is willing to cover
messages.issue: Listing 'what your insurance company is willing to cover' as one of the four things the rating affects reads as a coverage-decision prediction, which is a hard compliance line even though the rest of the email is a clean stage-1 curiosity build.
messages.recommendation: Reword to something the company can actually confirm, e.g. 'whether your rating is on file the way your policy assumes' rather than what the insurer 'is willing to cover.'

messages.job: Standalone curiosity nudge repeating the mismatch idea on its own terms, independent of the paired email.
messages.does: Restates the installed-vs-record mismatch without referencing the email itself.
messages.quote: honestly, what's installed and what's on record don't always match. Same window, two different answers.

messages.job: Close the loop on where the mismatch actually shows up (renewal, inspection, storm season), still no pitch, still just relevance.
messages.does: Walks through the three places the mismatch surfaces, tells a brief renewal story, and closes with the correctly-named Review as a P.S. escape hatch.
messages.quote: the credit can be reduced or denied
messages.issue: 'The credit can be reduced or denied' predicts a specific insurance outcome tied to the reader's own wind-mit credit, which is a hard compliance line even though the stage-fit and the Review CTA are both done right.
messages.recommendation: Reframe around what the homeowner can confirm (does the record match the install) rather than what the insurer will do about the credit.

messages.job: Standalone reinforcement of the 'by then it's harder to fix' urgency beat, independent of the paired email.
messages.does: Restates the same idea in its own words without referencing the email.
messages.quote: most folks don't find out until renewal, inspection, or storm season. By then it's harder to fix.

messages.job: Last note before the rep makes the direct offer — close the loop on how homeowners vs. inspectors check the same window, and explain what the Review actually is.
messages.does: Explains the homeowner-vs-inspector gap, tells a brief relieved-customer story with no invented dollar figure, and clearly distinguishes the Review from an in-home visit, quote, or pitch.
messages.quote: That’s what the 15-minute Protection Profile Review is for. Not an in-home visit. Not a quote. Not a pitch.

messages.job: Final, direct ask after five days of relevance-building — offer the low-commitment 15-minute Review, correctly named, as the last touch.
messages.does: Makes a single, clearly-labeled offer for the Protection Profile Review and signs off.
messages.quote: last note. Want your Protection Profile Review? 15-min call:

summary.strategy: Turn a friend's referral into a booked in-home visit as fast as possible.
summary.angle: Your friend thought we should connect — want us to come measure your home too?
summary.momentum_break: Every message from the first touch onward — the sequence never does the relevance/curiosity job stage 1 calls for; it opens on a direct booking ask (SMS) or brand positioning (Email #1) instead.
summary.why: This is the clearest stage-1 mismatch in the batch: every SMS makes the whole message a direct booking ask on day 0, the welcome email opens with 'Here's what we do differently at Reece' (brand positioning before any curiosity is built), 'free in-home estimate/assessment' appears three times (banned phrase, wrong locked term), the email predicts insurance impact and home value outcomes, and the footer misstates 1972 as a Florida founding.

messages.job: Use the referrer's borrowed trust to feel relevant and warm; open the relationship, not close it, on the very first touch.
messages.does: Names the referrer, then asks to set up an in-home estimate as the entire message.
messages.quote: mentioned you might be looking into hurricane windows. I’m with Reece, we took care of their home and I’d love to help with yours. Want me to set up a quick in-home estimate?
messages.issue: A direct booking ask is the whole first message to a lead who has only just been referred — no curiosity or relevance beat first. Referral rapport is borrowed trust, not the same as a lead who already engaged with a calculator or estimate tool, so this doesn't qualify for the calculator/estimate booking exception.
messages.recommendation: Lead with a relevance/rapport beat (what Reece did for the referrer, or a reason it matters for this reader's home) before asking to book; save the booking ask for message 2.

messages.job: Follow-up on the first message's ask for a lead who didn't respond, without a known email on file.
messages.does: Repeats the direct booking ask and calls it a 'free in-home estimate.'
messages.quote: You can grab a time for your free in-home estimate here:
messages.issue: 'Free in-home estimate' is the banned 'free estimate' pattern, and it isn't the locked term (Window Estimate / Measurement Verification / Home Protection Assessment). It also skips the Protection Profile Review on a referral lead with no calculator/estimate already in hand.
messages.recommendation: Name the visit with a locked term and route through the Protection Profile Review first, or if going direct is intentional for referrals, drop 'free' from the phrasing.

messages.job: Thank the reader for reaching out via referral and make the topic feel relevant to them — not position the brand or ask for a booking yet.
messages.does: Opens with 'Here's what we do differently at Reece' and goes straight into brand positioning (what the visit includes, exact quotes, no high-pressure), asks to 'get on the calendar,' and closes with a footer that conflates the 1972 Winston-Salem founding with 'South Florida.'
messages.quote: Here’s what we do differently at Reece:
messages.issue: Reece-is-different brand positioning on the very first email to a stage-1 referral lead — no relevance/curiosity first. Also predicts 'insurance impact' and 'home value gain' as outcomes, offers a 'free 90-minute assessment' (banned phrase + wrong locked term), and the footer's '...since 1972' misstates history (1972 was NC; 2005 is when Florida began).
messages.recommendation: Replace the positioning-led open with a warm, relevance-first welcome (why this matters for their home, not why Reece is different), remove the outcome/value predictions, rename the visit correctly, and fix the footer to not imply a 1972 Florida founding.

messages.job: Follow-up booking reminder for a lead who has an email on file and already received the welcome email.
messages.does: Repeats the same 'free in-home estimate' booking push.
messages.quote: You can grab a time for your free in-home estimate here:
messages.issue: Same as SMS #2: 'free in-home estimate' is the banned phrase pattern and the wrong locked term, and it skips the Protection Profile Review on a referral lead.
messages.recommendation: Same fix as SMS #2.

messages.job: Same as SMS #1 for a referral where the referrer's name wasn't captured — use the fact of being referred as light rapport, not a close.
messages.does: Skips straight to asking to set up an in-home estimate as the entire message.
messages.quote: I heard you were referred to us for hurricane windows. I’m with Reece Windows & Doors, we’d love to help. Want me to set up a quick in-home estimate?
messages.issue: Same issue as SMS #1: the entire first message is a direct booking ask with no relevance/curiosity beat first, and without even a named referrer to lend rapport.
messages.recommendation: Same as SMS #1 — lead with relevance before the ask.

summary.strategy: Fast-track high-intent digital leads (people who searched for impact windows or Reece by name) straight to positioning and a booking ask, skipping the slower indoctrination sequence.
summary.angle: You're already doing your homework — here's the one question that separates a real evaluation from a quote-and-run visit, and what homeowners find after installation.
summary.momentum_break: SMS #2 (S04 SA5 ROI Stat, day 0) — the first hard compliance break, introducing a fabricated 10-15% premium-drop stat and 'pays for itself'; Email #2 repeats the pattern with an invented $1,200-$3,500/year savings range.
summary.why: E.7's fast-track strategy is correctly applied — positioning and booking pushes are appropriate here, unlike E.1-E.6. But the execution repeatedly invents insurance-savings numbers ('pays for itself,' a 10-15% premium drop, $1,200-$3,500/year) that aren't among the five allowed stats and cross the no-savings-promise/no-outcome-prediction hard lines, one SMS tells the reader to check their email instead of standing alone, and one email defaults to 'South Florida.'

messages.job: Confirm this is a high-intent lead by naming their city, then open a curiosity loop about wind mitigation classification — E.7 is allowed to move fast, but this first touch is still the relevance/curiosity beat.
messages.does: Names the reader's city and asks whether they know their classification, but states as fact that it 'determines your insurance coverage.'
messages.quote: It's the #1 thing that determines your insurance coverage and protection level.
messages.issue: Framing the classification as what 'determines your insurance coverage' is an outcome prediction — a hard compliance line even on a message whose stage-fit (city hook, reply ask) is otherwise appropriate for a high-intent E.7 lead.
messages.recommendation: Reframe as 'one of the first things insurers look at' rather than what determines coverage.

messages.job: Positioning through an ROI stat, appropriate for E.7's faster decision-stage track (SA5).
messages.does: Cites an 'average 10-15% drop in insurance premiums' and says the upgrade 'pays for itself.'
messages.quote: It's one of the few home improvements that actually pays for itself.
messages.issue: 'Pays for itself' is one of the explicitly banned savings phrases, and the 10-15% figure is a fabricated insurance-premium stat — the only allowed comparable number is the 7-15% DOE energy-savings stat, which this is not. Two hard-line compliance breaks stacked in one text.
messages.recommendation: Drop 'pays for itself' entirely and replace the premium-drop figure with the actual 7-15% DOE energy-savings stat, correctly attributed.

messages.job: Close out the SMS thread with a direct booking offer — appropriate for E.7's fast-tracked, decision-stage leads.
messages.does: Offers a booking link described as an 'honest estimate' rather than a named locked term.
messages.quote: If you'd like an expert to walk through your home and give you an honest estimate — no pressure, no obligation - grab a time here:
messages.issue: Booking directly is fine for E.7's fast track, but 'honest estimate' isn't one of the locked visit names (Window Estimate / Measurement Verification / Home Protection Assessment), and E.7 isn't one of the named calculator/estimate exception workflows, so the CTA should route through the Protection Profile Review by name.
messages.recommendation: Name the visit correctly, or route this CTA to the Protection Profile Review if E.7 leads haven't already completed a calculator/estimate.

messages.job: Same as SMS #1 for a contact with no city captured — a generic version of the credibility/city hook.
messages.does: Asks about window rating and states it 'determines your insurance coverage and protection level.'
messages.quote: it's the #1 factor that determines your insurance coverage and protection level
messages.issue: Same outcome-prediction issue as SMS #1.
messages.recommendation: Same fix as SMS #1.

messages.job: Position the one question that separates a real evaluation from a quote-and-run visit — appropriate positioning for E.7's decision-stage lead.
messages.does: Makes the positioning case (evaluate classification before quoting), but claims the classification 'determines how your insurer covers you after a storm,' and the P.S. offers a 'free in-home estimate' instead of a named locked term.
messages.quote: schedule your free in-home estimate here
messages.issue: 'Free in-home estimate' is the banned phrase and the wrong locked term (should be Window Estimate / Measurement Verification / Home Protection Assessment), and 'determines how your insurer covers you' is a direct outcome prediction — almost the exact 'how your insurer judges your home' pattern the compliance rule names.
messages.recommendation: Rename the visit correctly and remove 'free'; rewrite the insurer-coverage line to what Reece can actually confirm (the classification on file), not what the insurer will do.

messages.job: Standalone positioning nudge repeating the 'ask this question' idea on its own, driving toward the paired email.
messages.does: Restates the provider-test question, then tells the reader to 'check your email, I just explained why it matters.'
messages.quote: Check your email, I just explained why it matters.
messages.issue: 'Check your email, I just explained why it matters' is functionally the banned 'I just sent you an email' pattern — it makes the SMS a trailer for the email instead of standing on its own. It also repeats the outcome-prediction line ('determines your coverage').
messages.recommendation: Rewrite so the SMS carries its own complete thought without directing the reader to the email.

messages.job: Positioning around ROI (premium savings + home value) for a decision-stage E.7 lead — the right lever for this point in the sequence.
messages.does: Claims most insurers 'adjust your premium' and states homeowners save '$1,200 to $3,500 a year,' then defaults to 'South Florida' for the resale-value claim.
messages.quote: We see homeowners saving anywhere from $1,200 to $3,500 a year.
messages.issue: A specific invented savings range ($1,200–$3,500/yr) is both an unauthorized statistic and a direct premium-change prediction — two hard compliance lines in the same sentence, and the most severe finding in this batch. 'South Florida' also appears as the default market instead of {{contact.city}}.
messages.recommendation: Remove the invented savings range entirely; if an energy-savings number is needed, use the 7-15% DOE stat correctly attributed. Replace 'South Florida' with {{contact.city}}.

messages.job: Direct booking push naming real capacity ('slots open this week') as the reason to act now — appropriate urgency for E.7's fast track.
messages.does: Offers open estimate slots and promises to 'show you exactly what your insurance savings could look like.'
messages.quote: show you exactly what your insurance savings could look like
messages.issue: Promising to show 'exactly what your insurance savings could look like' is an outcome/savings prediction, on top of naming the visit as generic 'estimate slots' rather than a locked term.
messages.recommendation: Drop the savings-preview promise; offer to review protection level and next steps instead, and name the visit correctly.

summary.strategy: After the in-home appointment, this workflow sends a week of emails and texts from 'Mark from Reece' and the sales rep to recap the visit, answer the objections homeowners usually raise, and nudge them to act on the proposal already in their inbox.
summary.angle: Positioning plus rapport: 'we already did the hard part together at your kitchen table — here is why this proposal fits your home, and what it's quietly costing you to wait.'
summary.why: Two emails invent insurance-outcome and dollar-savings claims beyond the five allowed stats (a fabricated $2,400 premium drop and $140/month energy savings; a 'hundreds more per year' insurer claim and a pays-for-itself line), and one states the company's age as 50 years instead of 54. Two of four SMS also point back to the email, breaking the standalone-SMS rule. The stage-4 structure itself is sound; the compliance execution is not.

messages.job: Recap what was found at the appointment, keep the proposal warm, and open a channel for questions without re-educating or pushing further.
messages.does: Thanks the homeowner, introduces Mark as the behind-the-scenes contact, recaps the proposal's code-compliance and warranty points, and implies the project could be 'cash-flow positive' through insurance and energy savings without citing a number.
messages.quote: often make this project cash-flow positive when you factor in the insurance and energy savings
messages.issue: The financing line promises the project will be 'cash-flow positive' once insurance and energy savings are factored in — an unquantified savings/pays-for-itself promise, the same category as the 'saved you money each month' line Mark ruled a mechanical no_savings_promise fail (calibration item 9).
messages.recommendation: Cut the cash-flow-positive framing, or replace it with the DOE-backed 7-15% energy figure if a savings point is needed.

messages.job: Give a quick emotional touch after the appointment that stands on its own, separate from the email.
messages.does: Reassures the homeowner their home is 'in a strong position' and tells them to go check the proposal in their inbox.
messages.quote: Proposal is in your email whenever you are ready.
messages.issue: The SMS points straight at the email ('Proposal is in your email whenever you are ready'), making it a trailer for the email rather than a standalone message — the same class of violation as the 'Short version in a bit' finding (calibration item 1), only more explicit.
messages.recommendation: Drop the email reference; give the SMS its own complete thought and a direct reply or booking prompt instead.

messages.job: Give a quick emotional touch after the appointment that stands on its own, separate from the email (no-name variant).
messages.does: Same message as the 'Have First Name' SMS, minus the rep's name, and again tells the homeowner to check the proposal in their email.
messages.quote: Proposal is in your email whenever you are ready.
messages.issue: Same email-reference problem as the sibling branch: 'Proposal is in your email whenever you are ready' makes the text a pointer to the email rather than a standalone message.
messages.recommendation: Drop the email reference; give the SMS its own complete thought and a direct reply or booking prompt instead.

messages.job: Recap what was found at the appointment, keep the proposal warm, and open a channel for questions without re-educating or pushing further (non-objection branch, identical copy to the objection-tag branch).
messages.does: Same text as the Email 1 objection-tag branch: thanks the homeowner, introduces Mark, recaps the proposal, and implies the project could be 'cash-flow positive' via insurance and energy savings without a figure.
messages.quote: often make this project cash-flow positive when you factor in the insurance and energy savings
messages.issue: Same unquantified savings/pays-for-itself promise as the objection-tag branch of this email.
messages.recommendation: Cut the cash-flow-positive framing, or replace it with the DOE-backed 7-15% energy figure if a savings point is needed.

messages.job: Keep the door open for follow-up questions after the appointment without pushing anything.
messages.does: Thanks the homeowner for their time, normalizes having a lingering question, and invites a text reply — with no reference to the email.
messages.quote: Most people leave those appointments with at least one thing they want clarified after thinking it over.

messages.job: Use a real customer story to reinforce that acting on the proposal now tends to pay off, without inventing outcomes.
messages.does: Tells a story about another homeowner whose premium reportedly 'dropped by over $2,400' and whose energy bill fell '$140 a month,' plus an unspecified refinance value bump — specific dollar outcomes that are not part of the approved stat bank.
messages.quote: Her annual premium dropped by over $2,400.
messages.issue: This social-proof story invents specific dollar outcomes ($2,400 premium drop, $140/month energy savings, an unspecified home-value gain) not among the five allowed stats and effectively predicts an insurance-premium change — both hard-line violations. It also reads as a new, uncatalogued parable rather than one from the approved P1-P8 bank or an unembellished true story.
messages.recommendation: Replace the invented figures with the approved DOE 7-15% energy range, or tell the story without stating a specific premium/energy dollar outcome at all — describe the reaction and the decision, not the numbers.

messages.job: Reframe the 'we need to think about it' hesitation so the homeowner revisits the proposal's numbers instead of stalling indefinitely.
messages.does: Normalizes the hesitation, then reframes it from 'should we spend this' to 'how long are we comfortable losing this,' and points back to the proposal's own savings section.
messages.quote: It stops being “Should we spend this?” and becomes “How long are we comfortable losing this?”

messages.job: Get a direct, low-pressure read on where the homeowner stands.
messages.does: Asks a simple either/or question about whether they're ready to move forward or still thinking it over.
messages.quote: Most people are either ready to move forward, or just thinking it through a bit more.

messages.job: Answer the predictable post-appointment questions (timing, financing, HOA, install timeline) to remove friction toward a decision.
messages.does: Answers four FAQ-style questions but overstates the company's age ('over 50 years' / '50 years' instead of the correct 54) and implies the project pays for itself via a 'cash-flow neutral' financing claim without an approved figure.
messages.quote: many projects are close to cash-flow neutral from month one
messages.issue: Two compliance misses: (1) 'After 50 years doing this' / 'over 50 years' misstates the company's history — the correct figure is 54 years (founded 1972), never a rounded or different number. (2) 'many projects are close to cash-flow neutral from month one' is an unquantified pays-for-itself promise, the same category flagged in calibration item 9.
messages.recommendation: Fix '50 years' to '54 years' (or 'since 1972'); replace the cash-flow-neutral line with the DOE 7-15% energy figure or drop the claim.

messages.job: Use a real, ongoing cost-of-inaction argument (rising energy costs, the coming storm season) to compress the decision toward acting now.
messages.does: Claims a specific, invented insurance cost consequence ('hundreds more per year'), an unquantified 'offsets the monthly financing payment' outcome, and defaults to 'South Florida' instead of the reader's own market even though the message uses {{contact.city}} elsewhere.
messages.quote: Your insurance company is classifying your home in a risk tier that costs you hundreds more per year than necessary.
messages.issue: Predicts a specific insurance outcome (a risk tier that 'costs you hundreds more per year') — a hard-line violation with a figure outside the five allowed stats. Also promises financing 'often offset[s] the monthly payment within the first year' (pays-for-itself claim), and defaults to 'South Florida' instead of {{contact.city}} used elsewhere in the message.
messages.recommendation: Remove the risk-tier/premium claim entirely (Reece can document exposure, not predict the insurer's decision); replace 'South Florida' with {{contact.city}}; cut or requalify the 'offset the monthly financing payment' line.

messages.job: Get a final, low-pressure read on where the homeowner landed, days after the appointment.
messages.does: Asks directly whether they moved forward or the proposal ended up on the back burner, standing on its own with no email reference.
messages.quote: most people either move forward… or it ends up on the back burner.

summary.strategy: This workflow is plumbing: it takes whatever reply the agentic Decision Engine already composed and relays it to the contact by SMS or, if there is no phone number, by email.
summary.angle: None — there is no copy to angle. The message body and email subject are both raw merge fields (`{{inboundWebhookRequest.message}}` / `.subject`) filled in by another system at send time.
summary.why: The workflow does its one job (deliver the agentic reply on the right channel) and there is nothing in this file to audit — no fixed subject, preheader or body text exists to check against voice or compliance rules. The actual copy quality lives wherever the agentic system composes `inboundWebhookRequest.message`, which is outside this file's scope.

messages.job: Deliver whatever reply the Decision Engine decided on, on the channel the contact prefers.
messages.does: Passes the agentic system's message straight through with no fixed wording of its own.
messages.quote: {{inboundWebhookRequest.message}}
messages.issue: The body is entirely dynamic at send time — this file has no fixed text to grade. Compliance depends on what the agentic system writes into `inboundWebhookRequest.message`, which is not visible here.

messages.job: Deliver the same agentic reply by email when no phone number is on file.
messages.does: Passes the agentic system's subject and message straight through with no fixed wording of its own.
messages.quote: {{inboundWebhookRequest.subject}}
messages.issue: Same as the SMS branch — subject and body are both dynamic merge fields with nothing fixed to grade in this file.

name: I.AI-MAIL AI Mouth Dynamic Email Writer

summary.strategy: When a contact is tagged as needing an email follow-up, GPT writes a subject, preheader, body and CTA button for them from a handful of context fields, and the email sends automatically.
summary.angle: A single templated email that tries to do the whole funnel at once — relevance, curiosity, hope, positioning and urgency in six paragraphs — then a CTA button that books an Assessment.
summary.momentum_break: The body-draft prompt itself is the break: it instructs the model to write 'Relevance → Curiosity → Hope → Insight/positioning → Internal urgency' in one email, which is the entire buyer journey (stage #1 through #4) compressed into a single send with no knowledge of which stage the tagged contact is actually in.
summary.why: The prompt hard-codes positioning and urgency into every email this workflow sends, regardless of the contact's real stage, and the fixed template around the AI copy has an emoji in the CTA line and books an Assessment directly instead of the Protection Profile Review. Because the trigger is a generic 'needs-email-follow-up' tag (not a calculator or estimate flow), there is no guarantee the recipient is far enough along for positioning or a direct booking ask.

messages.job: Follow up on whatever the contact's open loop was, at whatever stage they're actually at.
messages.does: Runs a fixed six-paragraph structure — relevance, curiosity, hope, positioning, urgency, then a transition to booking — on every contact the tag reaches, then closes with an emoji CTA that books an Assessment directly.
messages.quote: 👉 {{contact.cta_button_text}}
messages.issue: Three problems: (1) the body-draft prompt forces positioning and urgency into every email this workflow sends, which is premature for a stage #1/#2 contact; (2) the rendered email uses a 👉 emoji before the CTA, banned in email; (3) the CTA books the in-home Assessment directly on a generic follow-up tag, not a calculator/estimate path the answer key allows to skip the Review.
messages.recommendation: Split the body prompt into a stage-aware version (drop the positioning/urgency paragraphs unless a stage-3+ signal is present), remove the emoji from the CTA line in the template, and route the CTA to the Protection Profile Review unless the contact already has a calculator or estimate on file.

summary.strategy: Routes an inbound customer-service or callback request to the right local office phone number, with a different text depending on whether that office is open right now.
summary.angle: None — purely logistical: who to call and when.
summary.why: Both branches do exactly the job a callback handler needs to do: tell the contact who is calling them (or who to call) and when. No selling, no positioning, no compliance issues found.

messages.job: Tell the customer their local office is connecting them right now.
messages.does: States that the market office is calling now and gives a callback number if the call drops.
messages.quote: Hi {{contact.first_name}}, connecting you with our {{contact.service_market_name}} office at {{contact.service_phone_display}}. They're picking up now. If the call drops, just call them back at that number.

messages.job: Tell the customer the office is closed and when to call back.
messages.does: States office hours and gives the direct number to call during those hours.
messages.quote: Hi {{contact.first_name}}, our {{contact.service_market_name}} office is closed right now (we're open Mon-Fri 8 AM to 5 PM ET). Call us at {{contact.service_phone_display}} during those hours and we'll take care of you.

summary.strategy: When a lead tags an objection after their appointment (price, timing, competitor, trust, complexity, spouse, worth-it, or shutters), this workflow runs a 4-5 message email+SMS sequence over 13 days that acknowledges that specific objection and reframes it, without re-pitching.
summary.angle: Feel-felt-found: validate the objection as reasonable, show why Reece is the exception, then invite the reader to keep the door open -- never argue, never re-sell.
summary.momentum_break: Every branch's first three messages are explicitly told to skip any scheduling CTA, and the fourth, closing message never actually names a next step either — e.g. one ends on 'Let's start there' with no link or reply instruction. Momentum builds relevance and rapport but never compresses into an actual ask, which is exactly Stage 4's job.
summary.why: Copy stays in-stage, but breaks compliance repeatedly, not as one-offs: banned 'in-house' crew wording 7+ times; 1972-NC/2005-FL conflation 6+ times; the Irma stat mis-stated (31% vs 31.9%) with fabricated causes 3 times; insurer-outcome/savings promises 10+ times ('No coverage,' 'guaranteed coverage,' 'instant insurance discounts'); 2 SMS reuse a different branch's script; 3 SMS lack a first name; 1 email has no matching prompt.

messages.job: Validate that money is tight right now so the price objection doesn't get argued with, then quietly reopen the door.
messages.does: Reframes the cost as a 'cost-cutter' and promises monthly savings before any real number is on the table.
messages.quote: But what if protection actually saved you money each month?
messages.issue: Mark's own ruling (calibration item 9) flags this exact preview line as a savings promise with no number behind it; the locked body doubles down with 'their windows pay for themselves faster than expected,' which is an unqualified payback claim outside the five allowed stats.
messages.recommendation: Replace the preview with a DOE-cited energy line (7-15% energy savings) or drop the money claim and lead with reassurance only, per Mark's suggested rewrite.

messages.job: Give a standalone, low-pressure text that keeps the price conversation open without repeating the email.
messages.does: Opens with the rep's name and first name, normalizes financial strain, and asks a CTA-context-driven question about the payment plan.
messages.quote: We've helped other homeowners set up monthly plans that cost less than a tank of gas.

messages.job: Make the monthly payment feel small by comparison, without repeating the savings claim from email 1.
messages.does: Uses a daily-coffee comparison to shrink the perceived cost; stays in reframe mode with no scheduling ask, as instructed.
messages.quote: Here's a funny thought: if skipping one daily coffee covered the cost of protecting your home, would you do it?

messages.job: Make the cost of waiting concrete for a price-sensitive reader without inventing numbers.
messages.does: Claims that waiting itself raises insurance premiums and energy bills, and the bridge instruction tells the writer to 'reference ongoing premium waste' -- an insurer-outcome claim with no source.
messages.quote: Every month you wait, you're paying higher insurance premiums, higher energy bills, and carrying the risk of storm damage that could cost ten times more than the upgrade itself.
messages.issue: Predicts that premiums are actively rising because of the reader's current windows and implies they will stop rising after the upgrade -- an insurer-outcome prediction the canon reserves for the five allowed public stats only, and 'ten times more' is an invented multiplier.
messages.recommendation: Cut 'higher insurance premiums' and the 10x multiplier; keep the storm-damage risk framed as a real, unquantified risk instead of a predicted premium change.

messages.job: Compress the decision with a concrete, low-pressure next step for a reader who has been on the fence about money for two weeks.
messages.does: Offers 'flexible payment options, seasonal incentives, and financing programs' but never states what to do next or provides a link -- the sequence ends on a feeling, not a step.
messages.quote: If protecting your home is something you want, we'll help you find a way to make it work.
messages.issue: This is the last message in a 13-day, 5-touch price sequence and it still has no booking path, no phone number, and no explicit next action -- only 'Let's start there.' A stage-4 reader needs a concrete next step, not another open invitation.
messages.recommendation: Give email 4 one explicit, low-commitment action (reply with a number, or a link to see payment options) instead of ending on sentiment alone.

messages.job: Validate that comparing quotes is smart, then plant doubt about what a cheaper quote leaves out.
messages.does: Does that with humor, then claims installers are trained 'in house' -- the banned crew phrase -- while otherwise staying in reframe mode with a closing question instead of a CTA.
messages.quote: We train every installer in house.
messages.issue: Canon crew wording is 'factory-trained, Reece-certified crews... never random subcontractors' and explicitly bans 'in-house crews.' This locked line uses exactly the banned phrase.
messages.recommendation: Swap to 'Every installer is factory-trained and Reece-certified -- never a random subcontractor,' matching GTD S1.4 verbatim.

messages.job: Standalone text offering to compare quotes side by side, branching on whether the lead already signed elsewhere.
messages.does: Structure A offers a no-pressure comparison; Structure B (already signed) owns the situation and offers to review the contract instead of arguing with the decision.
messages.quote: Understood on the contract, and no hard feelings. One thing worth doing either way: know exactly what it covers.

messages.job: Deepen doubt about a competitor's long-term reliability using the company's real track record.
messages.does: Claims 50+ years protecting Florida families and reuses the banned 'in-house' crew phrase; the live subject line is also a leftover copy of email 1's subject, not this email's own.
messages.quote: Reece has been protecting Florida families for over 50 years. Our installers are trained in-house — not "whoever shows up in a van."
messages.issue: Conflates the 1972 NC founding with Florida presence (2005, ~2 decades) and repeats the banned 'in-house' crew phrase. Also: the live subject field is a stale duplicate of email 1's subject, not this email's own ('When That "Great Deal" Stops Answering the Phone').
messages.recommendation: Say 'over two decades protecting Florida families' (or '50+ years in business, serving Florida since 2005'); fix the crew phrase; correct the GHL subject field to match the prompt's own subject.

messages.job: Show the math on why cheap costs more, using logic rather than fear.
messages.does: Claims the windows 'pay for themselves' every year and the bridge instruction tells the writer to 'emphasize ongoing premium reductions and avoided claims' -- an insurer-outcome promise with no source.
messages.quote: Reece windows don't just save energy — they save time, stress, and money every year they're in your home. That's why our customers call it "the one purchase that keeps paying for itself."
messages.issue: 'Keeps paying for itself' and the bridge instruction's 'ongoing premium reductions' are savings and insurance-outcome promises with no dollar figure or citation behind them -- exactly the kind of claim the canon limits to the five allowed public stats.
messages.recommendation: Replace with the DOE 7-15% energy figure (the one savings stat that is allowed) and drop the 'premium reductions' instruction from the bridge.

messages.job: Close the competitor sequence by offering to double-check their quote, compressing the decision without pressure.
messages.does: Offers 'to review your quote one last time' but the offer is never operationalized into a link, reply keyword or phone number -- it ends on 'let's lock it in and move it off your to-do list' with nothing to click or reply to.
messages.quote: So let's make this easy: I'll have our team review your quote one last time and make sure you're getting the best possible value — apples to apples, warranty to warranty.
messages.issue: Last message of the competitor sequence still has no explicit next step or booking path after 13 days and 5 touches.
messages.recommendation: Add one explicit action: 'Reply with your competitor's quote and I'll send the comparison back today.'

messages.job: Validate a busy schedule as the real reason for delay and reframe protection as something that removes a task, not adds one.
messages.does: Does that, but the locked copy claims windows are installed by 'our in-house, Reece-trained teams' -- the banned crew phrase.
messages.quote: Reece handles everything — from measurement to installation to service — all with our in-house, Reece-trained teams.
messages.issue: 'In-house' is explicitly banned crew wording (GTD S1.4); the correct phrase is 'factory-trained, Reece-certified crews... never random subcontractors.'
messages.recommendation: Rewrite to 'all with Reece-trained, factory-certified crews -- never random subcontractors.'

messages.job: Standalone reassurance that the process is turnkey for a busy reader.
messages.does: Delivers exactly that, first-person team voice, with a low-pressure question.
messages.quote: I know life's busy, that's exactly why our process is turnkey.

messages.job: Show the reader they are already carrying the problem mentally, without pricing or urgency.
messages.does: Stays purely observational as instructed; no compliance issues.
messages.quote: Truth is, "later" is the most expensive word homeowners ever use.

messages.job: Make the cost of delay tangible for a busy reader without alarmism.
messages.does: States as fact that every month without protection means 'higher insurance premiums' -- the same unsupported premium-outcome claim as the price sequence.
messages.quote: And every month that passes without protection means higher insurance premiums, more energy waste, and another storm season closing in.
messages.issue: Predicts insurer pricing behavior with no citation -- an outcome prediction, not one of the five allowed stats.
messages.recommendation: Drop 'higher insurance premiums' or replace with the DOE energy-waste figure only.

messages.job: Reinforce the 'later never comes' idea and offer a light next step.
messages.does: Does exactly that in the reader's own voice-of-mind, standalone.
messages.quote: Hey {{contact.first_name}}, quick thought: "later" doesn't really happen.

messages.job: Close the timing sequence by making the next step feel effortless, with a concrete way to say yes.
messages.does: Repeats the Florida-for-50-years conflation and ends on 'Ready when you are' with no explicit action.
messages.quote: We've been protecting Florida families for over 50 years, and we've gotten pretty good at making it effortless.
messages.issue: Same 1972 NC / 2005 FL conflation as COMP-E02: the company is ~54 years old, but Florida presence is about two decades. 'Ready when you are' also leaves the final message of the sequence without a concrete next step.
messages.recommendation: Say 'in Florida for two decades' and add one explicit low-commitment action to close the sequence.

messages.job: Fully validate skepticism about contractors before making any claim of its own.
messages.does: Validates first, then correctly uses canon crew wording ('factory-trained... never random subcontractors') rather than 'in-house.'
messages.quote:
We don't use random subcontractors.
Every installer works directly for Reece and is factory-trained by the people who build our windows.

messages.job: Standalone reassurance that installers are trained and the warranty is real.
messages.does: Delivers that in team voice with a single question.
messages.quote: That's why we use only Reece trained installers and back everything for life.

messages.job: Show structurally (not just with marketing claims) why Reece doesn't disappear like a subcontractor-based competitor.
messages.does: Makes the process/accountability case, but the locked line 'stays in-house from start to finish' is the banned crew phrase.
messages.quote: Every project stays in-house from start to finish.
messages.issue: Repeats the banned 'in-house' crew phrase (this email's own subject line, ironically, is 'The Only Contractor in Florida Who Doesn't Disappear' -- the copy undercuts its own claim of being different by using the same generic phrasing every competitor uses).
messages.recommendation: Rewrite to 'Every project stays with Reece-certified, factory-trained crews from start to finish -- never handed off to a subcontractor.'

messages.job: Let objective facts and track record build trust instead of marketing claims.
messages.does: States 'Over 50 years protecting Florida families' -- conflating the 1972 NC founding with the 2005 Florida start.
messages.quote: Over 50 years protecting Florida families.
messages.issue: 1972 is Winston-Salem, NC; Florida presence began 2005 (about two decades), never conflate the two per canon. '5 decades straight' BBB rating in the same list compounds the same error.
messages.recommendation: Say 'Over 50 years in business. Two decades protecting Florida families.'

messages.job: Reinforce trust and track record for a reader who has said 'I've been burned before.'
messages.does: Instead sends the exact 'I know life's busy, that's exactly why our process is turnkey' text used for the Timing branch's first SMS -- it addresses busyness, not trust, and does not mention crews, warranty or track record at all.
messages.quote:
Hey {{contact.first_name}}, it's {{custom_values.rep_name}} with Reece.
I know life's busy, that's exactly why our process is turnkey.
We handle every step for you.
messages.issue: This prompt is byte-for-byte identical to TIME-SMS-01. It answers the wrong objection: a reader who said they don't trust contractors gets a message about being busy, not one about reliability or the warranty.
messages.recommendation: Write a Trust-specific SMS 2 (e.g. reinforce the Double Lifetime Warranty or offer a recent-customer reference), distinct from the Timing branch's SMS 1.

messages.job: Close the trust loop with belonging rather than another sales push, inviting them to see the difference.
messages.does: Ends warmly on 'Let this be the moment you see what it's like to never worry again' with no explicit next step or booking path.
messages.quote:
You've been let down before.

messages.job: Lower perceived disruption by showing the process is controlled and predictable.
messages.does: Unknown with confidence -- the live subject/preview do not match any prompt in aiPrompts.

messages.issue: COULD NOT MATCH TO A PROMPT. This subject/preview appear nowhere in the 51 aiPrompts. messages.job: Make the one-day timeline tangible so the reader stops picturing a weeks-long renovation.

messages.job: Standalone offer to make the joint conversation easy.

messages.job: Make the cost of NOT having the spouse conversation tangible without guilt.

messages.quote: The One Conversation That Could Save You Thousands

messages.recommendation: Replace the subject with something that doesn't quantify savings (e.g. 'The Conversation Worth Having Sooner') and drop the wasted-costs claim.

messages.job: Standalone offer to schedule a time that works for both partners.
messages.does: Delivers that in team voice, first-name-opened.
messages.quote: Most couples tell us the hardest part was just starting the conversation.
