messages.quote: We'll set up a time that works for both of you to walk through everything together.
messages.issue: The offer to 'set up a time' is never operationalized -- no link, no reply instruction. Fourth and final message in the sequence.
messages.recommendation: Add a concrete reply-based or link-based next step for both partners.

messages.job: Break the 'we're probably fine' assumption and surface hidden risk for a reader questioning whether windows are worth it at all.
messages.does: Cites a distorted version of the Irma claims stat and adds a causal claim the source stat does not make, plus a soft insurability prediction.
messages.quote: The truth? That's what thousands of families said before Hurricane Irma — right up until 31% of their insurance claims were denied because of outdated or unprotected windows.
messages.issue: The only allowed version of this stat is '31.9% of Florida homeowner claims from Hurricane Irma went unpaid (Florida OIR)' -- this rounds it to 31% AND invents a cause ('because of outdated or unprotected windows') the OIR statistic does not attribute. 'Keeping your home insurable in a changing Florida market' later in the same locked block is also an insurer-outcome prediction.
messages.recommendation: Use the exact figure and wording -- '31.9% of Florida homeowner claims from Hurricane Irma went unpaid (Florida OIR)' -- without attributing the cause to windows, and drop the insurability claim.

messages.job: Standalone reinforcement of the same risk point from the email, in the reader's own words.
messages.does: Repeats the same distorted 31% figure.
messages.quote: But when 31% of Irma claims were denied, "fine for now" stopped being fine.
messages.issue: Same stat distortion as the email it follows (31.9% unpaid, per Florida OIR, mis-stated as '31% ... denied').
messages.recommendation: Use '31.9%... went unpaid' verbatim, or drop the number from the SMS entirely.

messages.job: Show that storm risk is not tied to proximity to the coast.
messages.does: Claims homes with Reece windows 'kept... their claims covered, and their insurance premiums low' -- a direct insurer-outcome and savings promise.
messages.quote: Families with Reece impact windows kept their homes sealed, their claims covered, and their insurance premiums low.
messages.issue: This predicts specific insurer behavior (claims paid, premiums low) as a result of the windows -- exactly the outcome prediction the canon bars; it is not one of the five allowed stats.
messages.recommendation: Replace with 'kept their homes sealed and protected' and drop the claims/premium language entirely.

messages.job: Reframe impact windows as a return on investment rather than a pure expense.
messages.does: Promises 'insurance discounts' and a 'return within just a few years' -- both outcome/savings promises with no figure attached.
messages.quote: Between energy savings, insurance discounts, and resale value, most homeowners see a return within just a few years.
messages.issue: 'Insurance discounts' and 'a return within just a few years' are unquantified savings/outcome claims. Only the DOE 7-15% energy figure and the 72 cents-per-dollar resale stat (Cost vs Value) are allowed, and neither is cited here with its source.
messages.recommendation: Cite the DOE 7-15% energy figure and the 72-cent resale stat by name, and drop the generic 'insurance discounts... return' language.

messages.job: Standalone reinforcement that the windows pay for themselves, offered as a light next step.
messages.does: Claims the windows 'often pay for themselves in energy and insurance savings' -- a savings promise -- and the locked text has no {{contact.first_name}}.
messages.quote: Quick fact: our windows often pay for themselves in energy and insurance savings.
messages.issue: Two separate failures: (1) no {{contact.first_name}} anywhere in the locked SMS text; (2) 'pay for themselves in... insurance savings' is an unsupported savings/outcome promise.
messages.recommendation: Add 'Hey {{contact.first_name}},' and replace the savings claim with the DOE energy figure only.

messages.job: Close the 'worth it' sequence with pride and ownership rather than another sales push.
messages.does: Does that reasonably well; no CTA at all is consistent with the rule ('Soft action only... no scheduling language'), though it means the sequence never offers a next step.
messages.quote: You don't have to live on the coast or expect a hurricane tomorrow to take action today.

messages.job: Agree that most impact windows aren't worth it, then differentiate Reece on substance rather than hype.
messages.does: Agrees and differentiates on engineering and crews, correctly using 'Reece-trained crews only — never random subcontractors' -- but claims '50+ years of proof from... Florida homeowners.'
messages.quote: That's not marketing. That's 50+ years of proof from thousands of Florida homeowners who trusted us to protect what matters most.
messages.issue: Same 1972 NC / 2005 FL conflation found elsewhere in this workflow: the company is ~54 years old, but Florida-specific trust is about two decades.
messages.recommendation: Say 'decades of proof from thousands of Florida homeowners.'

messages.job: Standalone reinforcement that Reece can help the reader compare quotes with confidence.
messages.does: Sends the exact 'still comparing quotes... line up your numbers side by side' Structure A text used verbatim for the Competitor branch's SMS 1 -- it answers a comparison objection, not the 'is it worth it' objection this branch is for.
messages.quote: Totally get it, you've got a lot on your plate. But if you're still comparing quotes, let's make it easy.
messages.issue: This prompt is byte-for-byte identical to COMPETITOR-SMS-01's Structure A. A reader who questioned whether impact windows are worth it at all gets a 'still comparing quotes' message, not a worth-it-specific one.
messages.recommendation: Write a distinct Worth Path B SMS (e.g. reinforce the engineering/crew differentiation from WORTH-E01.2) rather than reusing the competitor script.

messages.job: Clear up a specific misconception (impact glass flexes rather than shatters) for a reader already deep in the objection.
messages.does: This reads as a generic myth-debunking education email -- the kind of 'secret' reveal Stage 2 uses -- rather than compressing toward a decision, and the bridge instructs referencing 'claims eligibility,' an insurance-outcome claim.
messages.quote: It's not hype — it's physics, backed by engineering, testing, and 2,500 installs a year that prove it works.
messages.issue: Stage 4's job is to overcome the specific objection and compress the decision, not to re-educate from first principles the way Stage 2 does. The FLEX:BRIDGE instruction also tells the writer to 'reference how sealed openings protect claims eligibility' -- an insurer-outcome prediction.
messages.recommendation: Trim the physics lesson to one sentence and drop the claims-eligibility instruction from the bridge; spend the space compressing toward a decision instead.

messages.job: Redirect blame from the product to poor installation, building authority without attacking a competitor by name.
messages.does: Does that reasonably, but the locked line says crews are 'trained in house by our manufacturing team' -- the banned phrase, undercutting the email's own point about avoiding sloppy subcontractors.
messages.quote: Our installers are trained in house by our manufacturing team — the same people who build the product.
messages.issue: Banned crew phrase 'in house.' This is also the third email in a row of pure education (glass physics, then install quality) rather than compression toward a decision, which is a Stage-2 pattern, not Stage-4's job.
messages.recommendation: Say 'trained directly by our manufacturing team, never handed to a subcontractor' and move to a concrete next step by this point in the sequence.

messages.job: Standalone reinforcement that installer training, not glass quality, is what actually matters.
messages.does: Repeats the banned 'in house' phrase and has no {{contact.first_name}}.
messages.quote: Our crews are trained in house by the people who build the product.
messages.issue: Two failures: no {{contact.first_name}}, and 'in house' is the same banned crew phrase used repeatedly across this workflow.
messages.recommendation: Add 'Hey {{contact.first_name}},' and remove 'in house.'

messages.job: Anchor trust in longevity and proof to close the 'not worth it' sequence.
messages.does: Repeats the Florida/50-years conflation in both the subject and body.
messages.quote: For over 50 years, Florida families have trusted us to protect their homes — not because of clever ads, but because their neighbors told them, "It works."
messages.issue: Same 1972 NC / 2005 FL conflation as elsewhere in this workflow, here repeated in both the preview ('50 years and 2,500 families later — we're still Florida's trusted name') and the body.
messages.recommendation: Say 'For two decades, Florida families have trusted us.'

messages.job: Challenge reliance on shutters and surface the modern insurance-proof gap without fear tactics.
messages.does: States as fact what insurers require for coverage -- a direct outcome prediction -- and offers a shutter buyback with no stated end date.
messages.quote: insurers now want proof that your shutters were actually up during the storm. No photos. No footage. No coverage.
messages.issue: 'No photos. No footage. No coverage' states how an insurer will rule on a claim -- exactly the outcome prediction the canon bars ('never predicts... how your insurer judges your home').
messages.recommendation: Reframe as 'many insurers are asking for proof shutters were deployed' without predicting the coverage outcome.

messages.job: Standalone follow-up offering a shutter trade-in.
messages.does: Repeats the insurer-proof claim and adds a real deadline framing -- 'buying back shutters this month' -- with no stated real constraint behind the one-month window.
messages.quote: We're buying back shutters this month for homeowners ready to upgrade to full time protection.
messages.issue: 'This month' reads as a manufactured deadline on the buyback offer with no real constraint (storm season, install capacity) named -- the kind of countdown framing the canon treats as fake scarcity unless tied to a real, stated constraint.
messages.recommendation: Either name the real constraint driving the window (e.g. 'before storm season') or drop the month-based framing and make the buyback open-ended.

messages.job: Show, with real numbers, that shutter owners are disproportionately denied insurance claims.
messages.does: Uses a distorted version of the Irma stat, invents a detail the source statistic doesn't contain, and signs off with 'To guaranteed coverage' -- an explicit coverage guarantee.
messages.quote: 31% of Irma claims were unpaid. Guess who topped the list? Shutter owners.
messages.issue: The allowed stat is '31.9% of Florida homeowner claims from Hurricane Irma went unpaid (Florida OIR)' with no breakdown by shutter ownership -- 'shutter owners topped the list' is a fabricated detail on top of an already-rounded figure. The signoff 'To guaranteed coverage' promises an insurance outcome Reece cannot guarantee.
messages.recommendation: Use the exact OIR figure without the shutter-owner claim, and change the signoff to something like 'To protection you can prove.'

messages.job: Confront, without shaming, whether the reader actually uses their shutters, and offer the buyback as an easy alternative.
messages.does: Does that in a light, honest tone with no fear tactics; the buyback offer is not date-bound here.
messages.quote: Half the homeowners we talk to admit they "meant to," but ran out of daylight or energy.

messages.job: Close the shutter sequence with a confident, concrete trade-up offer.
messages.does: Promises 'instant insurance discounts' -- a specific, unsupported outcome/savings claim -- and the live message's subject field is a stale duplicate of email 3's subject, not this email's own ('We'll Buy Your Shutters, Because You Deserve Better').
messages.quote: You'll get instant insurance discounts and drop the proof problem for good.
messages.issue: 'Instant insurance discounts' both predicts an insurer outcome and promises a savings result with no figure or source -- a compound compliance failure. Separately, the live subject field ('Be Honest—Do You Actually Use Them?') is a leftover copy of email 3's subject rather than this email's own locked subject.
messages.recommendation: Drop 'instant insurance discounts'; describe only what Reece controls (the buyback credit and the windows). Fix the GHL subject field to match the prompt's own subject line.

summary.strategy: Re-open the conversation with cold leads using a low-pressure check-in, then rebuild relevance and curiosity through short stories and real external constraints (storms, code changes, installer capacity) before ever asking for anything more than a reply.
summary.angle: Documentation/protection-proof relevance ('the word unknown,' code drift, two homes/one storm) paired with real seasonal and capacity constraints, always with a booking escape hatch to the Protection Profile Review rather than a hard pitch.
summary.why: Every message stays inside Stage 1's rules and offers the Review only as a low-key P.S., never the primary ask — this is also the successor to S1.1-legacy, and the outcome-prediction and pressure problems from that version are gone here. Remaining gaps are minor: several emails default to generic 'Florida' instead of {{contact.city}}, and one P.S. names the Review informally instead of using the locked term.

messages.quote: Still on your radar, or did it drop off? Reply YES or NO, no wrong answer.
messages.recommendation: Test adding a real external constraint per F10 (e.g. storm season timing) rather than a plain check-in.

messages.job: Make the problem relevant through a short story, no pitch, no positioning yet.

messages.recommendation: Use 'Protection Profile Review' by name in the P.S. line, consistent with the sibling email.

summary.strategy: Win back a lead who went cold 90 days ago by warning them their home is at risk of a denied insurance claim if they don't act, escalating over 90 days to a final deadline.
summary.angle: Fear of a denied insurance claim tied to an 'unverified' classification, escalating from a soft check-in to explicit claim-outcome predictions and a manufactured final deadline ('Nuclear Close').
summary.momentum_break: By Email #1 (day 3) the sequence has already jumped from a soft relevance-only opener to explicit insurance-outcome predictions and pressure - the wrong direction for Stage 1 - and it never comes back down. The final SMS, internally named 'Nuclear Close,' compresses the ask like a Stage 4 flash sale.
summary.why: Repeatedly violates the no-outcome-prediction rule (claims determine payout/approval/denial), applies decision-compression 'Nuclear Close' pressure to a passive Stage 1 list where F10 says never compress, and never offers the Review, going straight to booking an in-home visit for a cold lead. Registry notes say it's superseded by S1.1 v2, and every step shows zero sends in 30 days — looks retired; worth confirming it's fully off, and its copy should not be reused if reactivated.

messages.job: Re-open the conversation with a low-pressure, standalone question - no pitch, no fear.
messages.does: Uses a pattern interrupt ('your file's still open') and asks a soft question about protection status.
messages.quote: still open. Want clarity on your home
messages.recommendation: Add a real external constraint per F10 (e.g. storm season timing) - this opener is fine on its own, but the emails that follow immediately abandon this low-pressure tone.

messages.job: Should still be building relevance/curiosity at low pressure - no pitch, no outcome claims.
messages.does: Opens with 'the worst possible moment,' claims the skipped step 'determines whether a storm claim gets approved, reduced, or denied,' and says insurers prefer the 'Unknown' classification so they can downgrade without discussion.
messages.quote: the part that determines whether a storm claim gets approved, reduced, or denied
messages.issue: Predicts a specific insurance claim outcome and insurer motive - a hard no_outcome_prediction violation - in the very first re-engagement email to a Stage 1 cold lead; also written in Mark's first-person voice pre-appointment, which canon reserves for Randy; never mentions the Protection Profile Review, going straight to 'the Assessment' for a cold, unqualified lead.
messages.recommendation: Cut every insurer-mindset and claim-outcome claim; reframe purely around documentation ('we document what's installed, the carrier decides'); route the ask to the Protection Profile Review, not straight to an Assessment; drop first-person Mark pre-appointment.

messages.job: Should still be building relevance at low pressure for a Stage 1 reader.
messages.does: States as fact that unverified homes get 'downgraded faster,' 'assigned lower payout eligibility,' and 'denied more often.'
messages.quote: unverified homes get: downgraded faster questioned more aggressively assigned lower payout eligibility and denied more often
messages.issue: States specific negative insurance outcomes as certain fact (payout eligibility, denial rate) - a repeat, escalated no_outcome_prediction violation; still first-person Mark pre-appointment; still no Protection Profile Review offered, only 'reply clarity.'
messages.recommendation: Remove all outcome/payout predictions; reframe on documentation and giving the homeowner a paper record, and invite the reply toward the Protection Profile Review by name.

messages.job: Should still be building relevance at low pressure for a Stage 1 reader.
messages.does: States 'Non-compliant = denied claims' as a certainty and says 'the payout is predetermined before the inspection.'
messages.quote: Non-compliant = denied claims
messages.issue: The most explicit outcome-prediction violation in the sequence - claims denial and a predetermined payout as fact; three emails in a row have now escalated fear with no de-escalation, the opposite of Stage 1's low-pressure requirement.
messages.recommendation: This entire 90-day fear ladder needs to be rewritten around F10 (external constraint + curiosity + a single low-commitment ask), not a payout-denial narrative.

messages.job: Should be a low-pressure re-ask, not a claim-outcome warning.
messages.does: Claims a single 'unverified opening' can 'collapse a storm claim.'
messages.quote: one unverified opening can collapse a storm claim.
messages.issue: Predicts a specific insurance-claim outcome in an SMS, continuing the same hard-line violation as the email track.
messages.recommendation: Reframe around documentation only, without a claim-outcome claim.

messages.job: Use the real storm-projection update as the reason to act, without predicting claim/payout outcomes.

messages.quote: that default determines: your payout your approval speed your scrutiny level whether your claim even survives the first 5 minutes
messages.issue: Multiple absolute claims about how insurers process a claim and predetermine payout - a repeated hard no_outcome_prediction violation; still first-person Mark pre-appointment; still no Protection Profile Review CTA (ask is 'reply storm').
messages.recommendation: Keep the real NOAA hook; remove every payout/approval/claim-survival claim and route the reply to the Protection Profile Review by name.

messages.job: Offer inspector availability as a real capacity constraint, without predicting insurer behavior.

messages.recommendation: Keep the capacity framing if it's real; drop the insurer-behavior claim; offer the Protection Profile Review before an in-home slot.

messages.job: Should be a respectful, no-pressure close to a passive Stage 1 sequence (compare S1.1's and S1.3's final messages).
